The Auto-connect and Lockdown mode settings can be found in the Android system settings, follow this guide to enable one or both.
1. After clicking on the \"Go to VPN settings\" button below, click on the cogwheel next to the \"Warren VPN\" name.
Auto-connect is called Always-on VPN in the Android system settings and it makes sure you are constantly connected to the VPN tunnel and auto connects after restart.
2. To enable Auto-connect, click on the toggle next to \"Always-on VPN\".
The Lockdown mode is called \"Block connections without VPN\" in the Android system settings. It helps minimize leaks, however it has some known limitations which you can read more about

3. To enable Lockdown mode, click on the toggle next to \"Block connections without VPN\".

Automatically connect to a server when the app launches.
Automatically connect the VPN when your device starts up.
Block all traffic if the tunnel drops, instead of falling back to the unprotected network.

This built-in feature prevents your traffic from leaking outside the VPN tunnel if your network suddenly stops working or if the tunnel fails: it blocks your traffic until the connection is reestablished.

The difference between the kill switch and lockdown mode is that the kill switch prevents leaks during automatic tunnel reconnects, software crashes and similar accidents. With lockdown mode enabled, you must be connected to a Warren server to reach the internet: manually disconnecting or quitting the app blocks your connection.
Route IPv6 through the tunnel. When off, IPv6 is blocked to prevent leaks.
When this feature is enabled, IPv6 can be used alongside IPv4 in the VPN tunnel to communicate with internet services.
IPv4 is always enabled and the majority of websites and applications use this protocol. We do not recommend enabling IPv6 unless you know you need it.
Reach devices on your local network (printers, NAS, casting) directly while everything else stays tunneled. Disabled while the kill switch is blocking.
This feature allows access to other devices on the local network, such as for sharing, printing, streaming, etc.
It does this by allowing network communication outside the tunnel to local multicast and broadcast ranges as well as to and from these private IP ranges:
Send DNS queries to your own resolvers instead of the Warren exit resolver. DNS always stays inside the tunnel.
When this feature is enabled it stops the device from contacting certain domains or websites known for distributing ads, malware, trackers and more.
This might cause issues on certain websites, services, and apps.
Attention: this setting cannot be used in combination with \"Use custom DNS server\".

Request a stable external port from the exit (BitTorrent, hosting).
Warren pins each exit\'s key on first use and refuses to connect if it changes. Reset the pins only if you expect a legitimate key rotation; the next connect re-pins.
Every Warren exit you previously connected to will be re-pinned on the next connection (trust on first use).
Until the new pins are established the substitution-detection guard is briefly down: an attacker who replaced an exit between resets would not be flagged on the first reconnect.
Single-hop is faster, but one relay then sees both your IP and your destination. Multi-hop splits them across two relays so neither sees both.
Multi-hop routes traffic through a separate entry relay so the exit never sees your IP. Pick the entry and exit countries below, or leave them automatic to let Warren choose.

To evade censorship, Warren disguises the tunnel as ordinary web browsing: on the network it looks like standard browser traffic to a regular website (HTTP/3 on port 443). Obfuscation cannot be turned off, as traffic that stands out is traffic that can be blocked.

DAITA (Defence against AI-guided Traffic Analysis) hides patterns in your encrypted VPN traffic. Even when encrypted, the data packets entering and leaving your device can be analyzed by AI to reveal your activity.

It adds network noise and makes all packets the same size, so it is much harder to tell which sites you visit or who you communicate with. Note: this increases network traffic and can reduce speed, latency, and battery life. Use with caution on limited plans.
